name: Null Object
intent: Replace a missing object with a harmless one that does nothing, so callers never need to check for null.
scenario: An order service writes log lines through a Logger. In some setups no logger is configured, and the service must still work.
problem: Where logging is optional, the logger can be null, so every place that logs has to check first. One forgotten check crashes the order service in production, and the null checks hide what the code is really doing.
solution: Give the service a Logger every time. When nothing is configured it gets a NullLogger: the same interface, with a log() method that does nothing. The service calls logger.log(...) without a condition. The decision of what to do about a missing logger is made once, where the logger is chosen.
pain: Every logging call is wrapped in if (logger != null)
A forgotten check crashes the order service
The real work is hard to see among the checks
Each new optional collaborator adds the same checks again
benefits: The service calls the logger without any condition
A missing logger cannot cause a crash
The choice is made once, where the logger is created
The null case is a class that can be tested like any other
whenToUse: A collaborator is optional and doing nothing is a correct behaviour
The same null check appears in many places
You want a safe default, such as no logging, no discount or an empty list
whenNotToUse: Doing nothing would hide an error, such as a missing payment gateway: fail fast instead
There is exactly one call site, where a single if is clearer
Callers need to know that the object is missing and react to it
pitfalls: A null object that returns success for a real operation lets mistakes pass silently
A null object with state (counting calls, for example) is no longer harmless
Mixing null objects and real nulls in one code base leaves both kinds of bug
A null object that is returned for different reasons makes it hard to tell why nothing happened

roles.label: Client
roles.description: Code that uses the collaborator and never checks whether it is real.

roles.label: Abstract object
roles.description: The interface the client depends on, here Logger with log(message).

roles.label: Real object
roles.description: The working implementation, such as a logger that writes to the console.

roles.label: Null object
roles.description: An implementation whose methods do nothing, used when the real object is absent.

quiz.question: A service checks if (logger != null) before every log call, in 40 places. Last week one check was missed and an order failed with a null error. What is the best fix?
options: Wrap the whole service in a try block and log the null error when it occurs
Always pass a NullLogger that does nothing when none is configured, and drop the checks
Add a unit test that fails when a logging call has no null check in front of it
Make the logger a global variable, so that it can never be null anywhere in the code
quiz.explanation: Handling the missing case once, with an object that does nothing, removes every check and every chance to forget one. A try block hides the problem, a test for each missed check is fragile, and a global makes the logger harder to replace.

quiz.question: When no payment gateway is configured, a team supplies a NullPaymentGateway whose charge() returns success. In production the setting is missing, and customers receive goods without paying. What was the mistake?
options: The null gateway should have returned a random result, so that testing is more realistic
The null object should have been created only once, and then shared by the whole system
The charge should have been retried several times, in case the gateway was only slow
Doing nothing is not a valid answer to a charge, so a missing gateway should fail loudly
quiz.explanation: A null object is right when doing nothing is a correct result, such as for logging. A charge that quietly succeeds hides a configuration error and loses money. Fail fast for operations that must happen.

quiz.question: A pricing method returns the best discount, or null if there is none, and four callers each check for null. What does returning a NoDiscount object, whose apply(price) returns the price unchanged, give you?
options: Callers apply the discount in one step, and the totals are still right when there is no discount
A faster method, because the object is cheaper to create than the checks it replaces
Protection from wrong discounts, because a NoDiscount can never be applied to an order
A way for callers to see why there is no discount, from a reason held in the object
quiz.explanation: No discount means the price stays the same, so an object that returns the price unchanged is a correct, harmless answer, and callers lose their branches. It does not make anything faster, and it does not carry a reason unless you add one.
